title: Cognitive Linguistics & Language Teaching

pts: Cognitive linguistics argues grammar isn't a separate, autonomous system, but emerges from and reflects general cognitive processes like categorisation and metaphor.
This contrasts with Chomskyan approaches, which treat syntax as a distinct, largely autonomous mental module.
This isn't necessarily a rejection of Universal Grammar — it's a genuinely different theoretical starting point.
points.who: George Lakoff and Ronald Langacker's foundational work

v: Two short position statements (written for this book); sentence pairs on cards

items: Present two short statements: a Chomskyan view (syntax is a specialized, largely autonomous system) and a cognitive view (grammar is symbolic, meaningful and built from general cognition and usage).
Give groups sentence pairs such as The glass broke / I broke the glass, or She sent a letter to Priya / She sent Priya a letter.
Groups explain the difference first in purely formal terms, then in terms of meaning and perspective.
Discuss which explanation would help learners more, and when.
Note that the two views are different starting points, not simply right and wrong answers.
Participants compare the same pairs in Kannada, Hindi or Telugu and notice how each language packages the event.
Support: provide both explanations for the first pair as a model.
Challenge: participants find a sentence pair that a meaning-based explanation struggles to account for.

lines: Formal: She sent Priya a letter is a double-object construction; the indirect object moves before the direct object.

Meaning-based: the double-object pattern tends to present the recipient as actually receiving something; compare She sent a letter to Bengaluru with the odd She sent Bengaluru a letter (Goldberg 1995).
T: Which explanation tells a learner why the second sentence sounds odd?
S1: The meaning one. A city cannot really receive a letter.
T: Unless ‘Bengaluru’ means the office in Bengaluru, and then it becomes possible.

body: Purpose: to contrast two theoretical views of grammar without taking sides. Content: two diagrams of the mind: on the left a separate box labelled ‘syntax’ beside other boxes; on the right an interconnected web linking ‘categories’, ‘metaphor’, ‘attention’ and ‘usage’, with grammar woven through it. Style: clean, neutral diagram. Board version: one box among boxes beside a web of lines.

items: Google Slides (free) to present the two views side by side.

blocks.x: Sentence-pair cards and a two-column chart on the board.

pts: Conceptual metaphor theory argues abstract concepts are systematically understood through concrete, embodied metaphor — 'time is money,' 'argument is war.'
This offers a powerful, systematic tool for teaching seemingly arbitrary vocabulary and phrasal-verb patterns.
Making these underlying metaphors explicit can make otherwise confusing idiomatic language genuinely learnable.
points.who: George Lakoff & Mark Johnson, "Metaphors We Live By"

v: Sets of idiom cards; three headings on the board

items: Write three conceptual metaphors on the board: TIME IS MONEY, IDEAS ARE FOOD and ANGER IS HEAT.
Give groups a mixed set of expressions on cards.
Groups sort each card into its metaphor family.
Groups add expressions from their home languages that seem to fit the same family, and note any that do not.
Each learner writes a short personal paragraph using three expressions from one family.
Use metaphors for emotions (HAPPY IS UP, SAD IS DOWN) with younger or lower-level learners.
Support: fewer cards, with a picture on each.
Challenge: learners find new examples of one metaphor in a newspaper or a graded reader.

lines: TIME IS MONEY: spend an hour, save time, waste time, a costly delay, I can’t afford the time.
IDEAS ARE FOOD: food for thought, half-baked idea, digest the information, swallow a story.
ANGER IS HEAT: boiling with rage, hot-headed, let off steam, simmer down.
S1: In Hindi also we say waqt barbaad karna, to waste time.
S2: Is anger hot in Kannada too? I will ask my grandmother.
T: So some metaphors travel between languages. Let’s find one that doesn’t.

blocks.x: Lakoff and Johnson (1980) describe these as systematic patterns of thought, not isolated phrases, and Kövecses (2010) discusses how some metaphors are widely shared while others vary between cultures.

body: Purpose: to show idioms grouped by an underlying metaphor. Content: three trees, each trunk labelled with a metaphor in capitals, each branch carrying an expression; small home-language leaves in a different shape on some branches. Style: warm, organic illustration. Board version: three headings with lists underneath.

items: Cambridge Dictionary (free) for idiom meanings and examples.

blocks.x: Hand-written idiom cards stored in envelopes for reuse.

pts: Prototype theory argues grammatical and lexical categories have a central, typical member and fuzzier, less typical edges, rather than sharp, rule-defined boundaries.
This helps explain why some grammar rules have so many genuine exceptions rather than being cleanly rule-governed.
This offers a more psychologically realistic account of how native speakers actually categorise, and misjudge, borderline cases.

v: Picture sets; a list of countable and uncountable nouns

items: Ask learners to draw ‘a bird’ in ten seconds; compare drawings.
Discuss why most drew a sparrow or crow rather than a penguin or ostrich.
Introduce the idea of a category with a typical centre and less typical edges.
Apply it to grammar: rank nouns from ‘very countable’ to ‘hardly countable’ (chair, apple, cake, rice, advice, information).
Discuss why some nouns, like cake and coffee, move between categories depending on meaning.
Apply the same idea to verbs of state and action (know, think, have, run).
Support: work with pictures and a three-point scale.
Challenge: learners find corpus examples of borderline uses (two coffees, a good education).

blocks.x: A continuum drawn by one class:

lines: Very countable: chair, pen, bus → apple, cake → coffee, paper → rice, water → advice, information (rarely countable in standard English)
T: Why can we say two coffees but not usually two advices?
S1: Because a coffee can be a cup, a thing you can count.

T: Yes. The grammar follows how we picture the thing. And in Indian English you will often hear advices or informations, which shows that the edges of the category are drawn differently in different varieties (Unit 74).

blocks.x: Rosch (1975) showed that people judge some members of a category as better examples than others, and cognitive grammarians apply the same idea to grammatical categories (Taylor 2003).

body: Purpose: to show a prototype category. Content: a target with a sparrow at the centre, a hen and a duck in the middle ring, a penguin and an ostrich at the edge; a second, similar target for nouns with chair at the centre and information at the edge. Style: bright, clear. Board version: concentric circles with words.

items: SkELL (free) to find natural examples of borderline uses [VERIFY current interface].

blocks.x: Concentric circles drawn on chart paper, with word cards moved around.

body: Rosch’s early work on colour categories drew on fieldwork with the Dani people of Papua (then called West New Guinea), whose language has only two basic colour terms. Her findings suggested that some colours are perceived as better examples than others regardless of vocabulary [VERIFY interpretation and date of fieldwork].

pts: Construction Grammar treats form-meaning pairings — constructions — rather than individual words and separate rules as the basic unit of language.
This directly supports Unit 5's lexical-chunk teaching approach with a full underlying theoretical framework.
This theory blurs the traditional grammar-vocabulary divide this series has otherwise treated as largely separate domains.

v: A short text (written for this book); highlighters

items: Explain that a construction is any pairing of form and meaning: a word, a chunk, or an abstract pattern with slots.
Show three examples: by the way (fixed), the more…, the more… (partly fixed), X let alone Y (patterned).
Learners highlight constructions in a short text.
Learners fill the slots of one pattern with their own content.
Link to chunk teaching from Unit 5: vocabulary and grammar lie on a continuum.
Learners collect constructions from a film or cricket commentary.
Support: highlight only fixed chunks.
Challenge: learners describe the meaning of an abstract pattern in one sentence.

lines: The more Kavya practised, the more confident she became. She could hardly speak in June, let alone give a speech. By the way, she won the debate in December.
the more X, the more Y: two things increase together.
X, let alone Y: Y is even less likely than X.
by the way: introduces a side point.

blocks.x: Goldberg (1995, 2006) argues that such patterns carry meaning in themselves. Learners who acquire the more…, the more… as a unit can use it productively with new content.

body: Purpose: to show that words, chunks and patterns form one continuum. Content: a horizontal bar from ‘fixed’ (by the way) through ‘semi-fixed’ (the more…, the more…) to ‘abstract’ (Subject Verb Object Object); jigsaw pieces with slots grow larger along the bar. Style: clean infographic. Board version: a line with three labelled points.

items: Just the Word (free) to explore the words that fill a pattern’s slots.

pts: Explicitly teaching the conceptual metaphors underlying idiomatic expressions can make large groups of otherwise arbitrary phrases systematically learnable.
This extends Unit 5's chunk-teaching principle with an explanatory mechanism for why certain chunks cluster together meaningfully.
This is a genuinely practical, classroom-ready application of an otherwise abstract-sounding theory.

v: Ten phrasal verbs with up and out; simple drawings

items: Draw two images: an arrow rising (up) and an arrow leaving a container (out).
Explain the core meanings: up for increase, completion or visibility; out for leaving, disappearing or becoming available.
Learners sort ten phrasal verbs by the meaning of the particle.
Learners guess the meaning of two new verbs using the particle.
Test recall a week later, and compare with an earlier set taught as a list.
Use in, on and at for time and place with younger learners.
Support: provide the core meaning beside each drawing.
Challenge: learners find exceptions and discuss whether they can be explained.

lines: up: eat up (completion), speak up (more volume), turn up (appear), save up (increase).
out: run out (disappear), find out (become known), sell out (none left), hand out (distribute).
T: What might the ink dried up mean?
S1: It finished. No ink left.
T: Good. Up for completion. Now what about work out?
S2: Find the answer? It comes out.

blocks.x: Boers (2000) and later studies collected in Boers and Lindstromberg (2008) report that explaining the motivation of such expressions can improve retention, although results vary by learner and item.

body: Purpose: to visualize the core meanings of two particles. Content: two panels; left: a rising arrow with small pictures (a full plate being finished, a volume dial turning, a person arriving); right: an arrow leaving a box with pictures (an empty ink bottle, a lightbulb, a sold-out sign). Style: friendly line drawings. Board version: an arrow up and an arrow out of a box, with words.

items: Quizlet (free plan) for spaced review of phrasal verbs grouped by particle.

blocks.x: A wall chart of up and out with learner-added examples.

pts: Cognitive linguistics supports teaching grammar through its underlying conceptual meaning, rather than as arbitrary formal rules.
This directly reinforces Unit 6's meaning-before-rule principle, now with a fuller theoretical grounding.
Visual and spatial representations of grammatical meaning (like Unit 6's timelines) reflect this embodied-cognition approach.

v: Timelines and simple drawings; example sentences

items: Choose a grammar point often taught as a formal rule, such as the present perfect or will versus going to.
Present a core meaning with a drawing (for the present perfect, a past event with a line joining it to ‘now’).
Give learners sentences and ask them to explain each choice through the drawing.
Learners create their own drawings for two sentences.
Only then, summarize the form.
Use the idea of distance for modals and hypothetical meaning: past forms create distance in time, reality or politeness (Could you…?, If I had…).
Support: provide ready-made drawings to match.
Challenge: learners explain a contrast in their home language and in English.

lines: I have lost my keys. The loss is linked to now: I still cannot open the door.
I lost my keys yesterday. The event is placed in a finished past time.
T: Look at the drawing. Why does ‘yesterday’ not fit with ‘have lost’?
S1: Because ‘yesterday’ is cut off from now.
T: Yes, and the present perfect is about the line to now.

blocks.x: This extends Unit 6’s principle of meaning before rule. Tyler (2012) discusses experimental studies of teaching English modals and prepositions through such cognitive explanations.

body: Purpose: to show grammar meanings as images. Content: a timeline with a past dot joined by a curved line to ‘now’ (present perfect) beside one with a past dot in a box (past simple); a second panel shows distance for can and could. Style: minimal, geometric. Board version: two timelines drawn with chalk.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) to create grammar visuals.

blocks.x: Timelines drawn on the board and copied into notebooks.

body: Keep drawings simple and consistent across the year. If the present perfect always has a curved line to ‘now’, learners begin to recognize the meaning from the drawing alone.

pts: Cognitive linguistics' emphasis on actual usage patterns pairs naturally with the corpus-based teaching from Unit 58.
Both approaches privilege real, attested language use over abstract, idealised grammatical rules.
This theoretical pairing offers one coherent, evidence-grounded alternative pedagogical framework.

v: Teacher activity; B2–C1 for the learner version
Access to a free corpus tool or printed concordance lines

items: Choose a cognitive explanation you plan to teach, such as out meaning disappearance.
Search a corpus for run out, die out or fade out.
Check whether the examples fit the explanation and note any that do not.
Refine the explanation, or add a note on exceptions.
Link to corpus-based teaching in Unit 58.
Learners check a metaphor family from point 2 in a corpus.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: We have run out of time.
The tradition has slowly died out.
The music faded out at the end.
She ran out of the room.

blocks.x: The last line is literal motion, which is the source of the metaphorical uses above it. Cognitive linguistics expects exactly this link between physical and abstract meanings, and corpus evidence shows how frequent each use actually is (Ellis 2002).

body: Purpose: to show explanations tested against real usage. Content: a teacher holding a card labelled ‘out = disappear’ beside a screen of concordance lines, with ticks beside most and a note beside one. Style: clean, realistic. Board version: a short list of sentences with ticks and one question mark.

pts: Cognitive linguistics needn't be adopted as the sole correct theory — it's one more genuinely useful lens within this series' principled eclecticism.
It offers particular pedagogical strength for vocabulary, idiom, and meaning-focused grammar teaching specifically.
This connects back to Unit 77's broader theoretical-pluralism argument — multiple compatible frameworks can each inform practice.

v: A list of ten teaching problems

items: List ten teaching problems, such as idioms, prepositions, fluency, pronunciation, motivation and writing organization.
For each, decide whether cognitive linguistics offers a strong, weak or no useful lens.
Compare with other frameworks from Unit 77, such as input, interaction and output.
Choose one problem where the cognitive lens is strongest and plan one lesson using it.
Discuss in a DIET session with faculty who teach grammar and vocabulary modules.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Idioms and phrasal verbs: strong lens (metaphor and particle meaning).
Prepositions: strong lens (spatial meanings).
Speaking fluency: weaker lens; interaction and practice frameworks help more.
Classroom anxiety: little direct help; affective research (Unit 22) is more useful.

blocks.x: Cognitive linguistics offers particular strength for meaning-focused vocabulary and grammar, which is why it fits within the principled eclecticism of Unit 25 rather than replacing other approaches.

body: Purpose: to position cognitive linguistics as one framework among many. Content: a toolkit with several labelled lenses (input, interaction, sociocultural, cognitive); the cognitive lens is held up to a card of idioms, making the pattern clear. Style: warm, practical. body: Pick five idioms or phrasal verbs from your next coursebook unit. Group them by an underlying metaphor or particle meaning, teach them that way, and check a week later how many learners remember them compared with a list you taught last term.

dek: Unit 82 of 100: how the mind organises grammar and meaning — a distinct, influential theoretical lens offering real, practical pedagogical implications.

aims.x: Why do we say in the morning but on Monday, run out of time but run into a friend? Many teachers answer ‘That’s just how English is’, and many learners conclude that English is a heap of arbitrary exceptions. Cognitive linguistics offers another answer: much of language is motivated by the way humans perceive, categorize and imagine the world. This unit introduces the main ideas of cognitive linguistics and turns them into practical classroom activities for vocabulary, idiom and grammar.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain the central claim of cognitive linguistics and how it differs from a Chomskyan view of grammar;
use conceptual metaphors to group and teach idiomatic vocabulary;
explain prototype effects in lexical and grammatical categories;
describe constructions as form–meaning pairings and link them to chunk-based teaching;
design meaning-first explanations of grammar using spatial and visual representations;
combine cognitive explanations with corpus evidence;
position cognitive linguistics as one useful lens within principled eclecticism.

why: Why this matters. This series has referenced Chomskyan Universal Grammar since Unit 6. Cognitive linguistics offers a genuinely different, complementary account worth understanding directly.

background.x: Since Unit 6, this book has mentioned Noam Chomsky’s view that humans are born with a specialized capacity for language, often called Universal Grammar, in which syntax operates as a largely autonomous system (Unit 86 returns to this in depth). From the late 1970s onwards, a group of linguists including George Lakoff, Ronald Langacker and Leonard Talmy developed a different starting point. Cognitive linguistics holds that language draws on general cognitive abilities, such as categorization, attention, perspective-taking and metaphor, and that grammar itself is meaningful (Langacker 2008). It is also usage-based: our knowledge of language is built up from the expressions we actually meet and use.

Three ideas matter most for teachers. First, conceptual metaphor: we understand abstract domains through concrete ones, so that TIME IS MONEY yields spend, save, waste and invest time (Lakoff and Johnson 1980). Second, prototype categories: categories have central and peripheral members rather than sharp boundaries, as Eleanor Rosch’s (1975) experiments on categories such as ‘bird’ and ‘furniture’ showed. Third, constructions: pairings of form and meaning at every size, from words and chunks to abstract patterns such as the ditransitive She gave him a book (Goldberg 1995).

Applied cognitive linguistics has produced a growing body of classroom research. Studies by Frank Boers and Seth Lindstromberg, among others, suggest that making the motivation of idioms and phrasal verbs explicit can help learners remember them (Boers 2000; Boers and Lindstromberg 2008). Andrea Tyler (2012) reviews experimental work on teaching prepositions and modals through their core spatial and force-dynamic meanings. Jeannette Littlemore (2009) discusses how metaphor and cognitive approaches can be applied to learning and teaching more broadly. As Unit 81 showed, these studies should be read critically: many are small and short term, and the evidence is promising rather than settled.

For Indian classrooms, cognitive linguistics has a special attraction. Learners already know two or three languages, each with its own metaphors and spatial categories. Comparing how Kannada, Hindi or Tamil express time, emotion or position with how English does can turn the home language into a resource for noticing, as NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 recommend (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Some metaphors are widely shared across languages; others are not, and those differences are exactly where learners need help.

items: Metaphor family set. A teaching set of ten expressions grouped by two conceptual metaphors, with home-language comparisons.
Meaning-first explanation. A drawing and a short explanation for one grammar point, tested with learners.
Corpus check. A note showing how a cognitive explanation was checked against corpus examples and refined.
Positioning statement. A paragraph explaining where cognitive linguistics helps and where other frameworks are more useful.
Which parts of English have you been teaching as ‘just exceptions’? Could any be explained?
How do your learners’ home languages express time, emotion or position differently from English?
When is a meaning-based explanation helpful, and when might it overload learners?
What evidence would convince you that metaphor-based teaching works in your classroom?
How would you explain the difference between Chomskyan and cognitive views to a colleague?
Which constructions would be most useful for your learners to learn as whole patterns?

terms.def: An approach to language that sees it as grounded in general human cognition and experience, and studies meaning through categories, metaphor and constructions.
A way of understanding one domain of experience in terms of another, reflected in everyday language, such as time as money in spend time or save time (Lakoff and Johnson 1980).
In Construction Grammar, a pairing of form and meaning at any size, from single words and chunks to abstract patterns such as She gave him a book.
An approach to grammar that treats language as a network of form–meaning pairings, or constructions, at every level of size and abstraction (Goldberg 1995).

A basic mental pattern formed through bodily experience, such as CONTAINER, PATH or UP–DOWN, that underlies the meaning of many words, for example the particles in in, out, up and down (Johnson 1987).

In cognitive linguistics, the non-arbitrary link between an idiom’s literal image and its figurative meaning, as in hit the roof reflecting ‘anger is heat rising’; making this link visible can help learners remember idioms.
The core, often spatial, meaning of a particle such as up or out, which cognitive linguistics uses to explain phrasal verbs; for example, up suggesting completion in eat up and fill up.
The most typical member of a category, such as robin for ‘bird’; cognitive linguistics shows that language categories have central and peripheral members.

The view that language knowledge is built from the expressions people actually meet and use, through general cognitive abilities such as pattern-finding (Tomasello 2003). It emphasizes frequency, exposure and meaningful use.
